nameStory: The Least Lithobius gets its "least" name because it's among the smallest members of its genus, with "microps" meaning "small-eyed" in Greek. Stone centipedes earned their common name from their love of hiding under rocks, logs, and other rocky crevices where they hunt for tiny prey. The name "Lithobius" literally means "stone life" - a perfect description of where you'll find these secretive hunters.
description: The Least Lithobius is a small, fast-moving centipede with a flattened, segmented body that's perfectly built for squeezing under rocks and through soil cracks. Like all centipedes, it has one pair of legs per body segment, giving it a distinctive scurrying gait when it darts for cover. These tiny predators typically measure less than an inch long and have a brownish coloration that helps them blend with soil and decaying matter. Despite being called a "centipede" (meaning 100 feet), they actually have only 15 pairs of legs - 30 legs total.

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than other stone centipedes, usually under an inch long with a delicate, narrow build

idTips.label: Flattened body
idTips.description: Body feels firm but flexible when gently handled, compressed from top to bottom like it's been slightly squished

idTips.label: 15 leg pairs
idTips.description: Count exactly 30 legs total - 15 pairs, with the last pair extending noticeably behind the body

idTips.label: Brown coloration
idTips.description: Ranges from light tan to darker brown, sometimes with a slightly glossy appearance that catches light

idTips.label: Quick movement
idTips.description: Moves in rapid, darting motions when disturbed, disappearing under cover faster than you can blink

idTips.label: Antennae length
idTips.description: Long, thread-like antennae that are constantly moving and feeling ahead as it explores

habitat: Look for Least Lithobius under rocks, logs, and leaf litter in moist woodland areas throughout New England. They prefer areas with consistent moisture but good drainage, often found in deciduous and mixed forests where organic matter accumulates. You'll also discover them under garden stones, woodpiles, and mulched areas around homes.

seasonality.spring: Active as soil warms, often found when turning over stones or logs during spring cleaning activities in gardens.
seasonality.summer: Most active period - easily spotted when moving rocks or disturbing leaf litter during hiking or yard work.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move deeper into soil and under larger, more permanent shelter as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep in soil, under large logs, or in root cellars and basements where they remain sluggish but alive.

funFact: Despite having 30 legs, centipedes never get tangled up because they move their legs in perfectly coordinated waves, like a living conveyor belt, and if they lose a leg to a predator, they can regenerate it during their next molt!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its larger cousins, the Brown Centipede and Garden Lithobius, but the Least Lithobius is noticeably smaller and more delicate. Memory trick: "Least" equals "littlest" - if it's tiny and under a rock, it's likely the Least Lithobius.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse centipedes with millipedes - centipedes have one pair of legs per segment and are predators, while millipedes have two pairs per segment and eat decaying plants. Also, despite their fearsome appearance, stone centipedes are actually beneficial garden helpers that eat pest insects.
compareHints: The Least Lithobius is significantly smaller and more delicate than its relatives the Brown Centipede and Garden Lithobius, which can grow much larger and have more robust builds. While all three share the same basic body plan and habitat preferences, the Least Lithobius has proportionally longer antennae for its body size. Its smaller size also means it can squeeze into tighter spaces that its larger cousins cannot access.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Brown Centipede is larger and more robust than its relatives the Garden Lithobius and Least Lithobius.
Garden Lithobius is distinguished from the Brown Centipede by its reddish-brown coloration and slightly smaller size, while the Least Lithobius is much smaller overall.
